title: Which word fills the blank?

beats.say: The first step in rotating a key is blank. Follow the pin three quarters of the way along the strip. Read the word under its tip. Which word will the sampler print?
Revoke. Lift that word into the blank. The sampler draws uniformly along the strip, so a wider stretch gives a word a better chance.
Leave the sampled word in place. Under it are the four scores that produced the strip. Fill a second blank by taking the highest score. Which word wins this time?
Create wins with a score of three. Taking the highest score at each step is greedy decoding.

Read the guide. Create a replacement key, deploy it, then revoke the old key. Our draw picked the last step first. Each answer now ends in a different word, so the model sees a different history when it scores the next token. Beam search keeps several histories around to see where they lead.

title: Follow a path instead of enumerating the tree

beats.say: At each position, the model supplies a conditional distribution given the prompt and every generated token so far. Multiply those conditional probabilities along a path to obtain its joint probability. Adding log probabilities gives the same ranking while avoiding long products of tiny numbers.
If a tiny probability rounds to zero, taking its logarithm loses the original score. Direct log-softmax can still give the finite log probability for that edge.
At every fork there are three choices. Three choices for three positions already give twenty-seven paths. With V choices at each of T positions, the bottom row has V to the power T leaves.

With a thirty-two-thousand-token vocabulary and one hundred positions, that's about three point two seven times ten to the power four hundred fifty. An end token can stop a path sooner, and a grammar can rule out branches.

In this finite-state model, two routes reach the hall. The foyer route arrives with probability point three and the stairs route with point two. From the hall, either arrival leads to the door with probability point eight or the window with point two. Which arrival should Viterbi keep? To find the most probable path, Viterbi can merge histories at the same state when all future transition probabilities match. Each continuation multiplies both scores by the same factor. Keep the foyer route. Through the door it scores point two four against point one six. A transformer can give those two prefixes different transition probabilities. Here the window gets point two after foyer, hall, and point seven after stairs, hall. For the window exit, the stairs route now beats the foyer route, point one four to point zero six. A KV cache can reuse work along a shared prefix. Each distinct history still needs its own prediction.
To sample a whole path, draw one conditional token at a time. This is ancestral sampling. The chance of following a particular path is the product of its edge probabilities.

title: Turn scores into one normalized row

beats.say: Each word has a raw score called a logit. Create has three and quota has negative one. Softmax turns all four scores into probabilities that sum to one. Which word will get the biggest share?

Create leads. Subtract three, the largest score, from every entry. The shifted scores are zero, negative point five, negative two and negative four. Now exponentiate. The first weight is one, and the others are smaller. Together they weigh about one point seven six.

Divide each weight by the full sum. Create gets about fifty-seven percent of the strip. Subtracting the same logit from all four scores scaled their weights by the same factor, leaving their shares unchanged.
A uniform draw at point seven five lands in revoke’s interval. That gives us one word. The rest of the sentence could still say to revoke the old key after deploying its replacement.

title: Keep overflow, masks and tiny log probabilities distinct

beats.say: Now supply logits one thousand, nine hundred ninety-nine and nine hundred ninety-eight. Direct exponentiation overflows ordinary floating-point math. Subtracting the maximum leaves zero, negative one and negative two, whose exponentials fit and produce about point six six five, point two four five and point zero nine zero.
The printed probabilities match the mathematical softmax of the original scores. Subtracting the maximum lets the computer calculate them with finite weights.

Compare the shifted scores zero and minus one thousand. Ordinary probability for the second token rounds to zero. Its logarithm then gives negative infinity. Direct log-softmax still gives minus one thousand. A deliberate negative-infinity mask also gives zero probability, but marks a token the policy actually forbids.
If every token is masked, this lab rejects the row rather than dividing zero by zero. Its actual code also rejects NaN and positive infinity.

title: Append the chosen token before asking again

beats.say: Greedy selects the largest score at the current position. The article’s first row selects create. Append that token to the prompt before looking at the next row.
In this supplied two-step fixture, the second scores are four for a period, one point five for then, and point five for after. Predict which token is appended next.

The period wins. The answer now reads, “The first rotation step is create.” The period adds punctuation. That uses the second and last score row in this example. A model can also generate an explicit end token. With identical logits and a fixed tie rule, greedy decoding repeats the same choice.
Numerical differences in the runtime can change those logits. The KV cache saves attention state for the prefix so the model can reuse it when scoring the next word.

title: Which opening is worth keeping?

beats.say: Finish “You should” in exactly two tokens. These are new probabilities. Read the probabilities beside each opening. Forty percent of the mass goes to the word ‘create’. Thirty-five goes to ‘first’, and the last quarter goes to ‘revoke’. If you can keep just one opening, which one gets the next turn?
Create. Its best next token is a period, with a one-in-five chance on that branch. Multiply the two edges. That whole path gets eight percent.

Rewind to the same three openings. This time keep two. Create keeps its slot, first gets the second, and revoke drops out. After first, create has a seventy percent chance. Which two-token path takes the lead?

The pair is ‘first create’. Thirty-five percent times seventy percent gives twenty-four and a half percent. A smaller first branch won because more of its mass stayed on one continuation. The period on the other branch was ordinary punctuation. Both paths ended at the two-token limit.

Start a new sentence with Mia. Each word counts as one token. Only an explicit end token, E O S, finishes a path. Set completed paths aside. Allow four generated tokens including E O S. Rank active prefixes by their cumulative log probabilities and break ties alphabetically.

title: Each edge scores a conditional choice

beats.say: Given the same prefix, the model assigns mass across its next-token choices. Opened receives the largest share, looked receives a little less, and slept receives the smallest. These supplied toy probabilities let us trace each branch.

After opened, the word the has conditional probability one half. How much of the original mass follows both words? Multiply its two edges. Forty-five percent times one half leaves twenty-two and a half percent. The same calculation in log space adds the two edge scores.

A period and an end-of-sentence token have different meanings in a tokenizer. We will use the explicit EOS marker for completion, so the search knows exactly when a candidate stops and how many generated tokens its score includes.

title: Keep several openings while pruning

beats.say: Beam search keeps a small set of active prefixes. At the first step, width two retains opened and looked. The shorter route beginning with slept falls below the cutoff, so later steps cannot extend that route in this run.

Width counts the partial sentences we keep after ranking. With two active prefixes, each prefix still gets its own next-token distribution. Compare every extension by its cumulative score before filling the two slots again.

A beam acts like a narrow moving frontier through the tree. Its surviving leaves are promising under scores seen so far. The frontier is a compute budget, and pruning makes the procedure an approximation to searching every sequence.

title: Expand the surviving lattice

beats.say: Opened branches to the or a, while looked branches to outside or up. Each prefix can also end here. The left number on each piece of type is the conditional probability. The right number includes the probability of reaching the parent.

Compare the two rows together. The leading unfinished prefixes are opened the and looked outside. Carry them forward. One expansion later, door inherits the score of opened the, and again inherits the score of looked outside.

At position four, opened the door reaches EOS with the strongest completed route in the width-two run. The children ending in again and quietly have used all four positions. Both are unfinished, and neither gets another expansion. The best words at each position can come from different sentences.

title: EOS turns a path into an answer

beats.say: Now run the same tree with width three. This separate run keeps slept alive, where it reaches EOS immediately. An EOS choice moves a candidate into the completed set. A retained unfinished prefix gets another expansion while a position remains.
In the width-three run, the completed paths include Mia slept and Mia opened the door. For slept then EOS, point two times point nine five gives point one nine.

For opened, the, door, then EOS, point four five times point five times point eight times point eight five gives point one five three. The short path therefore earns the higher joint probability in this fixture.

Completion criteria and length constraints define eligible outputs. Early stopping determines how long search continues and can change which candidates are discovered. Reaching a length limit can leave an unfinished prefix. Here EOS alone marks completion, and the four-token horizon ends expansion.
Here the search expands for four positions, saves every end-token path it sees, and ranks only those finished paths. A different stopping rule can change the set you compare.

title: Length normalization changes the comparison

beats.say: Compare the completed candidates from the width-three run. Joint probability favors the short path. Every extra conditional probability is at most one, so extra edges add nonpositive log terms and can pressure a raw-sum objective toward brief completions.
Divide each completed log score by its generated-token count, including EOS. This changes the objective from total sequence probability to average log probability per token.

Slept has log score about negative one point six six one across two generated tokens, giving mean about negative point eight three zero. Opened the door has log score about negative one point eight seven seven across four, giving mean about negative point four six nine.
The larger, less negative mean belongs to opened the door. The paths stayed the same. Changing the divisor reversed their order.

GNMT used a different length penalty, and libraries expose their own conventions. The formula belongs to the decoding policy. Tune it on development examples and check the resulting answer lengths alongside task quality.

title: How much work did the beam do?

beats.say: Freeze the width-two search right after the first word. We're holding two prefixes, Mia opened and Mia looked. Each has three possible next tokens. How many extensions will the search score at this step?

Six extensions. Four children continue the sentence. The other two finish it. We keep the two best unfinished paths, opened the and looked outside, and put both end-token paths in the completed set. Six scored, two carried forward.

Those same six edges can cost different amounts of memory. Both prefixes start with Mia. A runtime could copy the prompt's cached keys and values for each prefix. Or it could let both prefixes point to one copy. The next tokens still need their own state. We examined six extensions either way.

Now count every extension examined over the four generated positions. Width one examined eleven, width two examined eighteen, and width three examined twenty-five. Only width three kept slept long enough to score its end token. Here that changed the most probable completed sentence.
On real prompts, measure latency, memory and answer quality alongside the search count.

title: Two cutoffs on the same tree

beats.say: Run the same three-token tree twice. Both searches see A at one half, B at three tenths and C at two tenths. The left beam has room for two openings. The right has room for three.

Follow A into the second position. Its three children have conditional probabilities point eight, point one eight, and point zero two. Their inherited path scores are point four, point zero nine, and point zero one. B splits ten ways, giving each child just point zero three.
On the right, C also gets a turn. It splits its two tenths evenly. Each C child carries one tenth. Compare the four candidate scores on the right. Would A two make the top three?
A two drops to fourth. Both C children fit ahead of it. On the left, C was cut a step earlier, so A two is still in second place.
One token to go. A two has a single continuation. It keeps its whole path probability. Each other surviving prefix splits ten ways equally. Which beam can finish with the higher probability?

Width two wins with point zero nine. Width three tops out at point zero four. The wider beam spent two slots on C, then both of those paths split again. It had already lost the one path that kept all its mass.

title: Which length formula picks the longer answer?

beats.say: A raw path score cannot increase when that same prefix gains another conditional edge, because the added log probability is nonpositive. This does not rank arbitrary completed branches by length.

In a separate supplied tree, immediate EOS has probability point zero one, while create followed by EOS has probability point nine nine times point nine zero, or point eight nine one. The longer completion wins.

The article compares completed log scores negative one at length two and negative one point six at length five, counting EOS. Division by length gives negative point five and negative point three two, favoring the long candidate.

GNMT instead divides by the quantity five plus length, over six, raised to alpha. At alpha one, its scores are about negative point eight five seven and negative point nine six zero, favoring the short candidate. State the formula and stopping contract before tuning either objective.

title: How far does the repeated word fall?

beats.say: Suppose the model has just written create, and create leads again. Repeatedly picking the highest score can repeat a phrase. A repetition processor changes the logits of tokens already seen. Check whether the runtime counts the prompt when it builds that set.

Create leads with three, just ahead of deploy at two point eight. We have already used create. Divide its positive score by one point two. It falls to two point five. Deploy now wins at two point eight.
For a seen negative score, multiply by the same factor. Negative one becomes negative one point two. Both moves take the score to the left.

Zero stays zero. Apply the penalty once per distinct token. A token with a lower score can still be drawn. Its share can even grow if competing words lose more weight. In code, the penalty can push down a variable name on the very line that needs to use it again.

title: Change concentration while preserving the finite-score order

beats.say: For positive temperature T, divide every logit by T before stable softmax. A lower temperature increases finite logit gaps; a higher temperature shrinks them. In our original row, temperature point five gives create about point seven two one probability and entropy point six four seven nats.
At temperature two, create falls to about point four three eight and quota rises to about point zero five nine.

Entropy is negative the sum of probability times log probability, with zero terms contributing zero. Natural logs give nats. For this fixed row and mask, entropy increases as temperature increases. At two it reaches about one point one nine zero. The wider spread gives words like quota more chances to be drawn.

Inspect a different row: two, two, zero and a masked negative infinity. As positive temperature approaches zero, the two equal maxima each retain half the limiting mass. First-index greedy would pick only the first.

As temperature grows without bound, the three finite candidates approach one third each while the masked token remains excluded. A runtime’s zero-temperature API convention is separate from substituting zero into this formula.

title: Replay eight draws from the same row

beats.say: Keep the probability strip fixed for eight draws. Seed seven twice produces the same sequence in Python: create, create, revoke, then five creates. Changing the seed to twenty-one changes the sequence. Both rows on screen use seven and make the same calls in the same order.
Those eight draws all used the same row. In a generated sentence, the third word, revoke, would become part of the prefix. The model would score the fourth word using that changed history.

A seed initializes the sampler state. Model logits can also change with batching, accumulation precision, kernels or software versions; a near tie can then flip greedy selection without any random draw. Deterministic kernels and a fixed environment can support replay within their stated limits.
Record the exact model, tokenizer when available, prompt, settings, versions and stop reason, and check which controls the selected API actually supports.

title: Where does the probability mass go?

beats.say: Give the sampler exactly two places. Start with the four printed probabilities as exact inputs. Keep the two highest, create and revoke. Together they account for point nine one three of the strip.
To draw from just those two, stretch their part back to a full unit. Create now gets about sixty-two percent and revoke gets the rest. Each original share was divided by the same retained mass.
Try the flatter row below. Keep two again. The names stay the same. How much of the original mass do those two keep here?

Just point five three. Almost half the mass is gone. After dividing by point five three, create and revoke split this draw almost evenly. That's the tradeoff with a fixed rank cutoff. It counts tokens, even when the tokens carry very different shares.

Now follow an unfiltered sequence. Suppose that whenever its history is still free of tail tokens, the next position has a two-in-a-thousand chance of drawing one. The gray part is the probability of getting this far without a single hit. Each new position keeps point nine nine eight of what was gray.
After a hundred positions, about eighteen percent of sequences have had a hit. Extend the same process to five hundred positions. Will more than half have seen a tail token?

Yes. About sixty-three percent have seen one. The gray part is point nine nine eight to the five hundredth power. Everything else has had at least one hit. We counted tail tokens under a specified probability model. To count wrong answers, we'd have to grade the text.

title: Which word takes us past ninety percent?

beats.say: Top-p sampling, also called nucleus sampling, starts with the most probable word and keeps adding words until their combined probability reaches the threshold. Set the line at ninety percent. Create alone falls short. Add revoke and the pair reaches point nine one three.
Keep the whole blue segment, including the part past the line. Divide both shares by their total and you can draw from those two words.
Try the flatter row. The line stays put. Even after rename, the first three words cover only seventy-seven percent. Which word takes us across?
Quota. This time it takes all four words to reach the line. The guide has no step by that name. In another prompt, a rare word at the end of the strip might be the exact name you need.

title: Set a cutoff relative to the largest probability

beats.say: Min-p compares each probability with a fraction of the largest one. With base point one zero and peaked maximum point five six eight, the absolute cutoff is point zero five six eight. Rename at point zero seven seven survives; quota at point zero one zero does not.
For min-p, compare each individual word with the cutoff. Rename clears this line on its own. You do not have to add up the probabilities above it.

The flat maximum point two eight instead sets cutoff point zero two eight, admitting every candidate. The rule includes a token that lands exactly on the cutoff. As temperature rises, the finite-logit candidates approach equal shares. With a base below one, eventually they all pass, including quota.

title: Make equality, ties and zero mass explicit

beats.say: Inspect the boundary worksheet: point five zero, point two five, point two five and zero. Our lab excludes zero-mass candidates. Top-k two uses insertion order to keep create and revoke; a tie-inclusive runtime cutoff could keep rename too. Top-p point seven five stops after create and revoke.
Min-p base point five keeps all three positive tokens because the absolute cutoff is point two five.

At top-p one, retain every positive-mass candidate. At min-p one, retain every candidate tied with the maximum. The lab rejects top-k zero, while some runtime interfaces use zero to disable that processor. Unsupported parameters and an empty allowed set need explicit handling.
Record the chosen boundary convention rather than assuming an identical name means an identical implementation.

Filter the actual unrounded softmax values, not their printed labels. In the original four-logit row, the first three probabilities sum to about point nine eight nine six, below a top-p threshold of point nine nine. Their three-decimal labels can appear to sum to point nine nine zero.
Using that rounded worksheet as input would be a different policy. Keep full values through the comparison.

title: Recompute the pool after each processor

beats.say: Take a fresh row. A has point six zero, B point two five, and C point one five. Run top-k two first. That removes C. See the space it leaves at the end? A and B together occupy only point eight five of the original strip.

Renormalizing stretches those two pieces until they fill the bed again. The line stays at point seven zero. A now occupies point six divided by point eight five, about point seven zero six. Does the nucleus still need B?

A alone crosses the line. The final draw gives A the entire strip. Reverse the order on the original row. Before any stretch, A ends at point six zero. Top-p first needs B to reach point seven zero. Top-k two then keeps both.
The inputs and numeric thresholds match, while the intermediate denominator and final membership differ.

Our demonstration used temperature, then one filter, then renormalization and a draw. A production policy can compose more processors, with its own order, tie rules and minimum-candidate behavior. A changed operator order is a changed policy. Preserve that configuration in an experiment receipt before attributing an output difference to retrieval or to a new model.

title: Follow actual token bytes through a grammar state

beats.say: Suppose the output must be a JSON object whose first-step field is one of create, revoke or rename. A grammar matcher tracks the current prefix and tests the full decoded bytes of a candidate token.

One candidate token can cross several boundaries. Trace those byte transitions. The letters spell create. The quote closes the string. Only after the closing brace does this object accept the end token.
For the supplied row, quota has logit six, revoke four, create three and rename two. Without the constraint, quota wins. The enum grammar masks quota, leaving revoke as its largest allowed score.
That is valid syntax and an allowed enum value, yet the retained guide says the first step is create. A separately supplied guide-derived allowlist selects create; the grammar did not infer it.

Return to the emitted prefix. Its last token left the string open. The letters, quote and brace are all in the next candidate token. The token budget is exhausted before that token can be emitted. The returned text still ends at the opening quote. This small enum can use finite-state matching. Recursive structures generally need a stack, and the matcher must follow the actual tokenizer.

The returned prefix is legal so far. The object is unfinished, so EOS is blocked. Check the stop reason and completion status before consuming the result. Also check which grammar or schema features the matcher supports and how it handles an empty allowed set.

title: Valid strings can still have different probability laws

beats.say: A grammar mask also changes how probabilities are distributed across valid completions. In the article’s separate two-token tree, the first token is A with probability point four or B with point six. The only valid strings are A x and B y.
The model gives x after A probability point one, and y after B point nine. Both first tokens have a possible valid future.

A local first-token mask keeps A and B. At the next position, each prefix has only one grammar-valid continuation, which is forced by renormalization. The final local probabilities are therefore point four for A x and point six for B y.
Now compute the original joint valid masses instead: point four times point one is point zero four, and point six times point nine is point five four.

Conditioning the original model on a valid complete string divides those masses by their total point five eight. The probabilities become about point zero six nine and point nine three one. Both methods emit valid strings, with different frequencies.
Exact conditioning requires information about valid future probability mass; ordinary local masking does not supply it. State which distribution the generation policy actually produces.

title: Generate complete answers before scoring them

beats.say: Here are three complete answers. B has the largest generator log probability. Best-of-N generates N answers and scores each with an outcome evaluator. Compare the three supplied scores. Which answer does the evaluator prefer?

It selects the highest score, point nine six for A. B stays the generator’s favorite. Ranking and selecting changes the distribution of returned answers. Rejection sampling instead accepts proposals under an acceptance rule. Independent generator draws are one possible sampling design. Record the design you used.

An automated checker can replace a learned scorer when the task provides one. A finite test suite establishes its tested cases, and a formal proof checker checks a formal statement under its trusted assumptions. More candidates cost generation and evaluation work.
They can also offer more opportunities for a fallible scorer to prefer a mistake. Keep candidate identity, scoring source and complete task judgment together.

title: Which step gets credit for a mistake?

beats.say: Outcome supervision supplies one label for a complete solution. An outcome model may still read its whole reasoning; the single final label makes error localization a credit-assignment problem. Process supervision adds labels for intermediate steps with their preceding context.

A process score can look like a probability. Calibration needs separate evidence. Taking the minimum asks how weak the weakest step looks. Multiplying step scores uses a different rule and can change the winner.

The article assigns plan A the steps create, deploy and revoke, with process scores point nine five, point nine two and point nine eight. Plan B begins by revoking, then creates and deploys, with scores point zero five, point nine zero and point nine two.
Their outcome scores are point nine six and point seven two. The outcome maximum and the minimum-step rule both select A; B’s minimum exposes its bad first step.

Give B’s first step a score of point nine nine. Its new minimum is point nine zero, still below A’s point nine two. A wins again. Look at what B got credit for, though. It revokes the old key first. Grading that step against the guide catches an error the final ranking hides.

title: Which branch gets the next visit?

beats.say: In a thought tree each branch continues a partial solution by one reasoning step. Evaluate the proposed steps, then choose which states to expand, prune or revisit. In the original Tree of Thoughts experiments, the model itself judged which branches looked promising.

Watch A and B on the left. Breadth-first visits both before it goes down a level. On the right, depth-first follows A to a leaf, then backtracks to try another branch. If the evaluator prunes B, both searches lose the chance to visit its children.

Monte Carlo Tree Search uses earlier simulations to decide which branch to visit next. In methods such as RAP it selects a branch, expands it, simulates an outcome and sends its reward back up the path. Here A has eight visits and B has only two.

Add an exploration bonus to each mean reward. With weight one, take the log of the parent's visit count, divide by the child's visit count, then take the square root. B has both the higher mean and the larger bonus.
Its score is about one point six seven, ahead of A at point nine four. Choose B. This visit returns a reward of point two. Add it to B's reward total and count one more visit.

One point four across three visits gives a mean of about point four six seven. Send the same reward up to the parent. Four point six across eleven visits gives a mean of about point four one eight. Both averages are ready for the next selection.

title: Restore target mass after rejecting a draft

beats.say: Exact speculative sampling aims to accelerate a specified target policy while preserving its output distribution in ideal arithmetic. At one position, draw from the actual draft distribution q.

Accept a proposed token with the smaller of one and its target probability p divided by its draft probability q. Accepted proposal mass at that token is the smaller of p and q. A draft cannot propose a token to which its own distribution gives zero mass.

The article supplies target probabilities point six, point three and point one, and draft probabilities point eight, point one and point one. Accepted mass is point six, point one and point one, totaling point eight. Rejection probability is point two.

Take the positive part of target minus draft. The remaining masses are zero, point two and zero. Divide by their sum to get the residual draw: zero, one, zero. Every rejected draw goes to revoke. Adding that correction restores the target frequencies.

Redrawing from the original target on rejection gives create too much mass. It ends up at point seven two, while revoke falls to point one six and rename gets point one two. If the target and draft already agree, every proposal passes.

Apply the correction using the actual draft probabilities and the target probabilities after its temperature, filters and masks. That recovers the target’s frequencies across draws. Individual runs can still produce different text with the same seed.

title: Keep only the prefix whose verification remains valid

beats.say: The draft has already written create, a, key. The target can score all three proposed positions together because it knows the prefixes. It scores create after the prompt, a after create, and key after create a. Causal attention also gives one more distribution after the entire block.
Read the context down the left edge. The row for key is valid after create a. If a changes, the context for key changes too.

In a separate supplied block, the draft proposes create, a, key. Create has target probability point six and draft probability point eight; uniform point two accepts its point seven five ratio. At the next position, a has target point four and draft point eight.

Uniform point eight rejects a because its acceptance ratio is one half. Keep create. Discard a and key, including the tentative cache after the rejected position. Draw one replacement from the residual at that position. The next iteration starts with the new prefix.

In another iteration where every proposal passes, append a further token from the target row after the full draft prefix. A block of K proposals can yield one through K plus one output tokens before stop rules intervene. A greedy target uses a matching deterministic verification rule.
Actual speed depends on draft cost, acceptance, batching and verification kernels; measure it against the unchanged target policy rather than assigning a speedup from the block size.

title: Count the event that the task actually asks for

beats.say: Draw two thousand times from each fixed row. Greedy selects create every time. At temperature two, create takes about forty-four percent of the probability and comes up in about forty-six percent of the draws.
With top-p at point nine, the expected and observed shares are both close to sixty-two percent. Each bar counts how often one word came up.

For a separate authored whole-answer audit, take one hundred requested answers. Ninety-two start with the guide’s first word, but only seventy are judged fully supported and complete. Ten hit a length limit. Those are different events.

In another supplied cohort, eighty-five first-word matches accompany eighty supported complete answers and five length limits. The task rate improves from seventy to eighty percent while first-word agreement falls. Keep every requested identity in the denominator.

Save the prompt and retrieved passages with the model and runtime versions. Record the decoder settings, processor order, grammar version, seed and stop reason. Keep the grading rule with the answers it scored. Hold the decoder fixed when testing a retrieval change, so you can compare what the answers say under the same decoding policy.

title: A second run from Mia opened

beats.say: Come back to Mia with a beam of two. After ‘opened’, the model gives half its mass to the word ‘the’, and three tenths to the word ‘a’. Multiply each by the chance of reaching ‘opened’.
On the other branch, ‘looked outside’ has a joint score of point one nine two five. Right now, opened the and looked outside go on.
Move three tenths from the word the to the word a. Leave the end-token share, the looked branch, and the horizon fixed. Use the two empty slots. Which unfinished prefixes belong there now?
Opened a and looked outside. Opened a now carries forty-five percent times sixty percent, or point two seven. ‘Looked outside’ keeps its place. ‘Opened the’ has fallen to point zero nine.

Trace opened the toward its door. The break in that line marks where the beam cut it. Now follow opened a through book and the end token. The four edges multiply to point one seven zero one. This path wins on raw probability and on mean log probability, about minus point four four three per generated token.
The conditional probabilities after door were unchanged. That ending became unreachable one step earlier, when the beam lost opened the.

title: Would you accept this answer?

beats.say: Here's a different guide. Back up the current key, rotate it, then remove the old copy. The answer field accepts backup, rotate or remove. First we'll choose a word, then we'll check a finished answer.
On the original row, start with the biggest share. Include words until you have at least three quarters of the mass. Where do you cut?

After rotate. Backup and rotate together reach point seven eight, and both are allowed in the field. Divide by that retained mass. Backup now occupies about fifty-nine percent of the draw, rotate about forty-one.
Put the pin at point six five. Which word does the sampler write?
Rotate. That's a legal action, but it's step two in this guide. Keep the pin there. Change only the first-word rule to require the action at the start of the guide. Which word owns the pin now?
Backup. Our first-word rule leaves one candidate, so backup fills the whole strip. Now read this finished answer against the guide, one step at a time. Where does it first depart from the guide?

Step two. The answer says remove while the guide says rotate. Move remove after rotate and compare again. All three steps now match. When you test a retrieval change, hold the decoder fixed and grade each complete answer this way.
